Urban freeways on weekends do not appear to have poor data quality, but we see from other sections that they do, and thus the speed distributions may not be highly representative. A combination of the two day types could be applied to the urban freeway weekend distribution to augment data density, as in the file speedDistributionResults_byRoadHour_source.csv. As an alternative to this hourly resolution, we suggest combining across hours in the next section. Figure 38. Combined speed bin distributions for transit buses by hour Figure 39 displays the speed distribution for drayage trucks, which were one of two vocations in common across the two data sets. For late night and early morning hours of the day, we see a distinct, sharp peak at the speed bin centered on 60 mph on urban freeways. For midday and evening hours, we see a slightly slower peak split between 55 and 60 mph and more time spent under 40 mph. Weekend data on urban freeways are sparser, but we see some peaking at 60 mph, as well as some sharp 50- and 70-mph peaks for different hours of the day. On other urban roads, we see a predominant peak at 5 mph, with secondary peaks around 55 mph on weekdays and 60 mph on weekends. 49 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Combined speed bin distributions for drayage vocation of combination-unit short-haul by hour Lastly, we see the speed bin distribution for the towing vocation, which was found in both data sets within the single-unit short-haul source type. All categories have under 10 vehicles, and the urban freeway distribution appears messy. Overall, there seems to be generally increasing percentages from 0 to 60 mph, with some trucks in early morning hours even spending most of their time in the highest category speed bin, which is classified as 2-minute average speeds over 72.5 mph. Combined speed bin distributions for towing vocation of single-unit short-haul by hour In general, we observed 60-mph peaks on freeways, and most often 5-mph but also up to 30-mph peaks in speed bin distribution on other roads. We also saw that vehicles tended to move faster in hours around midnight, except for vocations like street sweepers and freeway work trucks, which may have been performing duties during those times. During the day, trucks sometimes had a smaller 60-mph peak on freeways and distributed their time over speeds under 40 mph slightly more.
